The transportation problem ships goods from $m$ sources with supplies $s_i$ to $n$ destinations with demands $d_j$ at unit cost $c_{ij}$, minimising $\sum_i \sum_j c_{ij}x_{ij}$. Its structure allows specialised methods:

items: Initial solution — North-West Corner Rule (simple, ignores costs), Least Cost Method, or Vogel's Approximation Method (uses penalty differences and usually starts close to optimal).

Optimality test — the MODI (u–v) method computes dual values $u_i + v_j = c_{ij}$ on occupied cells and checks reduced costs $c_{ij} - u_i - v_j$ on empty cells; a negative value signals an improving loop.
Assignment problem — a special case with one-to-one allocation (workers to jobs), solved efficiently by the Hungarian method of row and column reductions.

body.text: Two-person zero-sum games are also closely linked: finding a player's optimal mixed strategy can be written as an LP, and the two players' problems are a primal–dual pair.

body.title: In practice
body.text: We build LP models for production planning, distribution networks, workforce rostering and media budget allocation. The solver is rarely the hard part; agreeing on the objective, collecting reliable cost and capacity data, and explaining shadow prices to decision-makers is where the value lies. Sensitivity analysis — how far each cost or capacity can change before the plan changes — is a standard part of our deliverable.

title: Decision Analysis Under Uncertainty and Risk
summary: Decision analysis provides a structured way to choose between actions when the outcome depends on states of nature we cannot control. This article compares the standard criteria for decisions under uncertainty, expected monetary value under risk, the value of perfect information, decision trees with Bayesian revision, and Monte Carlo simulation.

body.text: Many business choices — whether to expand capacity, launch a product or commission a survey — share a structure: a set of possible actions, a set of states of nature beyond the decision-maker's control, and a payoff for each action–state pair. Decision analysis makes this structure explicit so that the choice can be argued transparently rather than by intuition alone.
The payoff matrix

Rows are actions $a_i$, columns are states $\theta_j$, and entries are payoffs $v(a_i, \theta_j)$, often profits. The running example below is a firm deciding how to respond to uncertain demand. Payoffs are in lakh rupees, with probabilities to be used later.
Decisions under uncertainty
If no probabilities can be assigned, several standard criteria are available, each encoding a different attitude to risk:

items: Maximin (Wald, pessimistic) — for each action find the worst payoff and choose the action whose worst case is best.
Maximax (optimistic) — choose the action with the largest best-case payoff.

Minimax regret (Savage) — regret is $r_{ij} = \max_k v(a_k, \theta_j) - v(a_i, \theta_j)$, the opportunity loss of not having chosen the best action for that state; choose the action whose maximum regret is smallest.
Laplace (equal likelihood) — treat all states as equally likely and choose the action with the highest average payoff.
Hurwicz — a weighted blend $\alpha \cdot \text{best} + (1-\alpha) \cdot \text{worst}$ with an optimism coefficient $\alpha$.

body.text: Decisions under risk: expected monetary value
When probabilities $p_j$ for the states can be estimated from data or expert judgement, the standard criterion is expected monetary value (EMV), equivalently minimising expected opportunity loss:

EVPI is the most a rational decision-maker should pay for a perfect forecast, and it equals the minimum expected opportunity loss. It is an upper bound on the worth of any real study, survey or pilot.

body.title: Worked example: applying the criteria
body.text: Use the payoff matrix above.
steps: Maximin: worst cases are −60, 10, 30, so choose No expansion (30).
Maximax: best cases are 200, 120, 30, so choose Large expansion (200).
Regret: column maxima are 200, 80, 30. Maximum regrets are 90 (Large), 80 (Small) and 170 (None), so minimax regret chooses Small expansion.
Laplace: averages are 220/3 ≈ 73.3, 200/3 ≈ 66.7 and 30, so choose Large expansion.
EMV: Large $= 0.3(200) + 0.5(80) + 0.2(-60) = 88$; Small $= 36 + 35 + 2 = 73$; None $= 30$. Choose Large expansion.
With perfect information: $0.3(200) + 0.5(80) + 0.2(30) = 106$, so EVPI $= 106 - 88 = 18$ lakh.

body.text: The example shows why the criterion must be agreed before the analysis: four reasonable rules recommend three different actions.
Decision trees and Bayesian revision

Sequential decisions — for example, first deciding whether to commission a market survey and then deciding on expansion — are drawn as decision trees. Square nodes are decisions, circles are chance events and leaves carry payoffs. The tree is solved by backward induction: at chance nodes take the expected value, at decision nodes take the best branch.
When an experiment yields an indicator $s$ (such as a 'favourable' survey), the prior state probabilities are revised with Bayes' theorem before the downstream decision is evaluated:

body.caption: Posterior probability of a state after observing survey result $s$

body.text: Comparing the expected value of the tree with and without the experiment gives the expected value of sample information (EVSI); the experiment is worthwhile if EVSI exceeds its cost. EVSI can never exceed EVPI.
Monte Carlo simulation

When payoffs depend on several uncertain inputs (price, volume, cost, timing), closed-form expectations become awkward. Monte Carlo simulation draws each input from its probability distribution, computes the payoff, repeats thousands of times, and summarises the resulting distribution: its mean, its percentiles, and the probability of a loss. This shows not only the expected outcome but also the downside risk that EMV hides.

body.title: In practice
body.text: We use payoff tables and decision trees to structure investment, pricing and capacity decisions with management teams, and Monte Carlo models when the inputs are numerous or correlated. Often the most useful output is EVPI or EVSI: it tells a client whether a proposed market study or pilot is worth its cost before money is spent. Sensitivity of the recommended action to the probability estimates is always reported alongside the answer.

title: Matrix Decompositions for Data Science
summary: Factorising a matrix into simpler pieces is how linear systems, least-squares fits, PCA and recommender models are actually computed. This article reviews LU, Cholesky, QR, eigenvalue and singular value decompositions, the power method, and why conditioning matters for numerical accuracy.

body.text: A data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ with $n$ rows (observations) and $p$ columns (features) is the starting point of almost every statistical model. Rather than inverting matrices directly — which is slow and numerically fragile — numerical software factorises them into products of triangular, orthogonal or diagonal matrices that are easy to work with. Knowing which decomposition sits under a routine helps explain its speed, accuracy and failure modes.
Gaussian elimination and LU

Gaussian elimination reduces a system $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ to upper-triangular form by row operations, then solves by back substitution. Recording the multipliers gives the LU factorisation:

body.caption: LU with partial pivoting: unit lower-triangular $\mathbf{L}$, upper-triangular $\mathbf{U}$, permutation $\mathbf{P}$

body.text: Once $\mathbf{A}$ is factorised (about $\tfrac{2}{3}n^3$ operations), each new right-hand side costs only two triangular solves, $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$. Partial pivoting (swapping rows to use the largest available pivot) is essential to control round-off error.
Cholesky for symmetric positive definite matrices

Covariance matrices and the normal-equations matrix $\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}$ are symmetric positive definite (when of full rank). For these, $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{\top}$ with $\mathbf{L}$ lower-triangular with positive diagonal. Cholesky needs half the work of LU, needs no pivoting, and fails exactly when the matrix is not positive definite — a useful diagnostic.

body.title: Worked example: solving a system by Cholesky
body.text: Solve $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b} = (6,\ 5)^{\top}$.
QR and least squares

Any $n \times p$ matrix of full column rank can be written $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$, where $\mathbf{Q}$ has orthonormal columns and $\mathbf{R}$ is upper-triangular. Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation builds $\mathbf{Q}$ column by column (the modified version is more stable); Householder reflections are the standard, most robust method in software.
For the least-squares problem $\min \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} \rVert_2$ there are two routes:

body.caption: Normal equations (left) and the QR approach (right)

body.text: The normal equations are fast but square the condition number, $\kappa(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}) = \kappa(\mathbf{X})^2$, so precision is lost when predictors are nearly collinear. QR works with $\mathbf{X}$ directly and is what statistical packages typically use for linear regression.
Eigenvalue decomposition and the power method

A symmetric matrix has a spectral decomposition $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^{\top}$ with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors — the computation behind PCA. When only the dominant eigenvalue is needed, the power method repeatedly multiplies a starting vector by $\mathbf{A}$ and normalises: $\mathbf{v}_{k+1} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_k / \lVert \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_k \rVert$. The Rayleigh quotient $\mathbf{v}_k^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_k$ converges to $\lambda_1$ at a rate governed by $\lvert \lambda_2/\lambda_1 \rvert$. For the matrix in the example above, starting from $(1, 1)$, three iterations give 5.562, matching the exact $\lambda_1 = (7 + \sqrt{17})/2 \approx 5.5616$. The same idea underlies PageRank.
Singular value decomposition

body.caption: SVD: orthogonal $\mathbf{U}$, $\mathbf{V}$ and non-negative singular values on the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$

body.text: The SVD exists for every matrix. The number of non-zero singular values is the rank; in floating point, the numerical rank counts singular values above a tolerance, revealing near-dependence among columns. Truncating to the $k$ largest singular values gives the best rank-$k$ approximation (Eckart–Young), which is the basis of PCA on centred data, latent semantic analysis, image compression and many recommender systems. The SVD also gives the pseudo-inverse for rank-deficient least squares.
Condition number and sensitivity

body.caption: 2-norm condition number and the error amplification bound

body.text: A condition number near 1 (orthogonal matrices) is ideal; one of $10^k$ means roughly $k$ significant digits can be lost. The matrix in the worked example has $\kappa \approx 5.562/1.438 \approx 3.87$, which is very well conditioned.

body.title: In practice
body.text: When a client's regression gives unstable or absurd coefficients, we check the condition number and singular values of the design matrix before anything else; near-collinearity is usually the cause. Choosing QR or SVD over explicit inverses, using Cholesky to simulate correlated scenarios, and truncated SVD for large sparse data are small engineering decisions that make analytical pipelines both faster and more trustworthy.

title: Numerical Root-Finding Methods
summary: Most equations met in modelling cannot be solved in closed form, so their roots are found by iterative numerical methods. This article explains error types, bracketing and open methods from bisection to Newton–Raphson with worked iterations, orders of convergence, and briefly introduces interpolation and numerical integration.

body.text: Finding $x$ such that $f(x) = 0$ is one of the most common computational tasks. It appears when solving for an internal rate of return, an equilibrium price, a maximum-likelihood estimate (where the score function is zero) or the steady state of a model. Except for special cases, such as polynomials of low degree, the answer must be approximated by iteration.
Errors in numerical computation

items: Round-off error — computers store numbers with finite precision (about 16 significant digits in double precision), so every arithmetic operation may introduce a tiny error that can accumulate or be amplified, for example when subtracting nearly equal numbers.
Truncation error — the error from replacing an infinite process by a finite one, such as stopping an iteration or cutting off a Taylor series.
Absolute and relative error — if $\tilde{x}$ approximates $x$, the absolute error is $\lvert x - \tilde{x} \rvert$ and the relative error is $\lvert x - \tilde{x} \rvert / \lvert x \rvert$.

body.text: Bracketing methods

If $f$ is continuous and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, the intermediate value theorem guarantees a root in $[a, b]$. Bisection evaluates the midpoint and keeps the half-interval where the sign change persists. It is slow but certain: after $n$ steps the error is at most $(b - a)/2^n$.
Regula falsi (false position) replaces the midpoint with the point where the chord joining $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$ crosses the axis:
It keeps the bracket, so it always converges, and it is usually faster than bisection, though one endpoint can stagnate on strongly curved functions.
Open methods

The secant method applies the same formula to the two most recent iterates rather than a bracket; it converges faster (order about 1.618) but can fail if the iterates wander. Fixed-point iteration rewrites the equation as $x = g(x)$ and iterates $x_{k+1} = g(x_k)$; it converges near a fixed point when $\lvert g'(x) \rvert < 1$ there, linearly with rate $\lvert g'(x^*) \rvert$.
Newton–Raphson linearises $f$ at the current iterate using its tangent line and jumps to where the tangent meets the axis:

body.caption: Quadratic convergence near a simple root

body.text: Quadratic convergence means the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step once the iterate is close. The cost is the need for the derivative, and the method can fail if $f'(x_k)$ is near zero or the starting point is poor.

body.title: Worked example: solving x³ − x − 2 = 0
body.text: Here $f(x) = x^3 - x - 2$ and $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1$. Since $f(1) = -2 < 0$ and $f(2) = 4 > 0$, a root lies in $[1, 2]$.
steps: Bisection: midpoints 1.5 ($f = -0.125$), 1.75 ($f \approx 1.609$), 1.625 ($f \approx 0.666$), 1.5625 ($f \approx 0.252$), 1.53125 ($f \approx 0.059$) — after five steps the root is known to lie in $[1.5, 1.53125]$.
$x_3 \approx 1.5213797068$, with $\lvert f(x_3) \rvert < 10^{-13}$: three Newton steps reach full double-precision accuracy, while bisection would need about 50 halvings.

body.text: Comparing the methods

A robust practical strategy combines them: bracket the root, take Newton or secant steps, and fall back to bisection whenever a step leaves the bracket. Library routines such as Brent's method follow this philosophy.
Related topics: interpolation and integration

The same numerical-methods toolkit includes interpolation — fitting a polynomial through tabulated points using Newton's forward and backward differences or Lagrange's formula — and numerical integration. The trapezoidal rule approximates an integral by trapezoids, with error proportional to $h^2$; Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas through pairs of sub-intervals, with error proportional to $h^4$:

body.tex: \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{h}{3}\left[ f_0 + 4(f_1 + f_3 + \cdots + f_{n-1}) + 2(f_2 + f_4 + \cdots + f_{n-2}) + f_n \right]
body.caption: Composite Simpson's 1/3 rule ($n$ even, $h = (b-a)/n$)

body.title: In practice
body.text: Root-finding sits quietly inside many analyses we deliver: solving for break-even volumes and internal rates of return, inverting cumulative distribution functions, and maximising likelihoods via Newton-type algorithms. When a model fails to converge, understanding these methods — scaling, starting values, bracketing — is what turns an error message into a working estimate.

title: Time Value of Money: Interest, Annuities and Gradients
summary: A sum of money available today is worth more than the same sum in the future, and interest is the tool that converts between the two. This article covers simple and compound interest, effective rates, present and future value, annuity and gradient series factors, and growth and decay curves.

body.title: Educational content
body.text: This article explains standard mathematical formulas for teaching purposes. It is not financial, investment, tax or legal advice; consult a qualified professional before making financial decisions.

The time value of money rests on a simple observation: money available now can be invested to earn a return, so a rupee today is worth more than a rupee promised in a year. Interest is the price of that delay. Every comparison of cash flows at different dates — a loan schedule, a project appraisal, a lease-versus-buy decision — begins by moving all amounts to a common date.
Simple interest and simple discount

Under simple interest at rate $r$ per period, interest is earned only on the original principal $P$, so after $t$ periods the amount is $A = P(1 + rt)$. Simple discount works from the other end: a sum $F$ due in $t$ periods is discounted at rate $d$, giving discount $D = Fdt$ and proceeds $P = F(1 - dt)$. Discount is computed on the maturity value, which is why a discount rate implies a slightly higher equivalent interest rate.

steps: Simple interest: ₹10,000 at 8% per year for 3 years earns $10000 \times 0.08 \times 3 = 2400$, giving ₹12,400.
Compound interest: the same sum at 8% compounded quarterly is $10000(1.02)^{12} \approx 12682.42$, i.e. ₹12,682.42. The effective annual rate is $(1.02)^4 - 1 \approx 8.243\%$.
Annuity: five year-end payments of ₹2,000 at 10% have present value $2000 \times \frac{1 - 1.1^{-5}}{0.1} = 2000 \times 3.79079 \approx 7581.57$, i.e. ₹7,581.57.
Interpretation: compounding adds ₹282.42 over simple interest in three years, and receiving ₹10,000 spread over five years is worth about ₹7,582 today at 10%.

When $i = g$ the formula reduces to $P = nA_1/(1 + i)$.
Growth and decay curves

The same mathematics describes growth and decay more generally. Discrete compounding $y_t = y_0(1 + g)^t$ and continuous growth $y(t) = y_0 e^{kt}$ model population, revenue or prices; with $k < 0$ the curve describes depreciation, radioactive decay or the fading effect of advertising. The doubling time under continuous growth is $\ln 2 / k$, and the familiar 'rule of 72' approximates the doubling time under annual compounding at $r$ percent as about $72/r$ years.

body.title: In practice
body.text: We apply these factors when building cost–benefit and project appraisal models, comparing equipment replacement options, structuring repayment schedules in planning tools, and teaching analysts to audit spreadsheet financial models. The most common errors we find are mismatched periods (a monthly payment with an annual rate) and confusion between nominal and effective rates — both are caught by writing every cash flow on a timeline before applying any formula.
